newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Bangui mutineers seek dialogue after bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Bangui mutineers seek dialogue after bloodshed.

text.p: Army mutineers in the Central African republic called for dialogue after a weekend of bloody clashes with French forces, who launched helicopter-led raids to avenge the killing of two French officers.

With Mali's former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure expected in Bangui on Monday on a fresh mediation mission, French forces held new strategic positions after the raids which killed at least 10 mutineers.
"I think that it (dialogue) is necessary. If we had wanted a bloodbath I think we would have opted for that this morning," a rebel spokesman told Radio France International.

"I think it would be preferable for each side to stay in their positions overnight pending the negotiations that will open with the return of General Toumani Toure," the spokesman, who gave his name as Lieutenant Mbeaye, said.

The Central African Republic is in the grip of its third army revolt in a year. French troops, in the former colony under a defence pact, intervened to keep President Ange-Felix Patasse in power during the second revolt in May.
France accused mutineers of gunning down the two unarmed officers on Saturday and said Sunday's raids, which also used tanks and armoured personnel carriers, were in self-defence.
A French military spokesman in Bangui told reporters French troops had wrested control from the mutineers of the port and its fuel supplies and a short-wave state radio transmitter.
"Our aim is not to put down the mutineers, our aim is to ensure that the Central African Republic can continue its democratic process," a French Foreign Ministry spokesman said.
Witnesses said French helicopter gunships fired on the mutineers' command posts in Kassai army camp, their sole remaining bastion, and other areas of the capital.
A French defence ministry spokesman said 10 mutineers were killed and 30 were taken prisoner.
Spokesmen for the mutineers put the death toll among their ranks at 21 and said 11 civilians had also been killed around their headquarters in the populous southern district of Petevo.
Calm returned to the city later in the day but residents reported an exodus of civilians from rebel areas.

Hundreds of people have been killed in violence associated with the revolts, which began in April. Initially about pay, they have turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a civilian elected in 1993 during the country's democratic transition.
Witnesses said three civilians were killed on Saturday when French troops and mutineers clashed in Bangui after civilians supporting the mutineers tried to move towards the city centre.
The latest revolt began on November 16.
